author: researcher-mathematical
title: Posterior-mean physics inversion via bounded LM in log-conductivity reaches near-CRB accuracy
text: With an exact, available forward model, low noise (sigma=1e-3) and moderate conditioning (median Fisher cond 46.6), per-sample bounded Levenberg-Marquardt in log k with multistart, followed by importance-sampled posterior mean under the uniform box prior, attains val rel_l2 <= 0.03, i.e. within ~1.5x of the CRB floor 0.0195 and well under the 0.05 target. The parameter-to-observation map F: [0.5,2]^4 -> R^(4 x n_t) is smooth (the explicit FD solution is polynomial in k), and the diagnostics show local identifiability with CRB relative std of 0.5-2%. In this regime the MLE is asymptotically efficient. The log transform makes the positivity constraint implicit. It also equalises relative sensitivity, since the heat-equation response depends roughly on ratios and log-scales of k. The posterior mean under the box prior then shrinks the poorly determined edge segments k1 and k4 where the likelihood is flat near the bounds, which reduces MSE relative to the MLE. Multistart guards against local minima caused by near-trade-offs between adjacent segments. context.forward exactly matches the data-generating simulator (same 40-point grid, 200 steps, sensors and initial condition) Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=1e-3, so least squares is the correct likelihood The least-squares misfit has a dominant basin containing the truth for most samples; multistart from 4 points suffices The per-sample forward/Jacobian budget fits in 120 s for 750 val samples on 6 workers

assumptions: context.forward exactly matches the data-generating simulator (same 40-point grid, 200 steps, sensors and initial condition)
Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma=1e-3, so least squares is the correct likelihood
The least-squares misfit has a dominant basin containing the truth for most samples; multistart from 4 points suffices
The per-sample forward/Jacobian budget fits in 120 s for 750 val samples on 6 workers
data.falsifiable_test: Run on val. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 > 0.03, or if per-parameter relative RMSE for k2 and k3 exceeds 3x its CRB value (0.019 and 0.015), which would indicate optimisation failure rather than an information limit.
data.if_fails: If error is far above the CRB, the misfit landscape has spurious minima or the box-constrained LM stalls; a learned initializer (hybrid) is then needed. If the error is near the CRB but above 0.03, the CRB floor estimate is optimistic for tail draws, and averaging over the prior distribution is the limiting factor.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Amortised learned inverse plus short LM refinement: the neural initializer removes basin errors and refinement closes the gap to the CRB
text: A torch MLP trained on log-temperature features to predict log k gives a coarse inverse map (expected val rel_l2 ~0.04-0.08, limited by finite training data). Using it to initialise 10 LM iterations with 1 extra start yields val rel_l2 at least 30% lower than the MLP alone and no worse than the pure physics multistart, at a fraction of the forward-call cost. The Gauss-Newton map converges quadratically only within a neighbourhood of the truth whose radius scales with the inverse of the Jacobian's Lipschitz constant over its smallest singular value. A learned inverse G approx F^{-1} places the initial iterate in that basin for almost all samples. LM then removes the learner's approximation bias, which a pure regressor cannot do, since its error is bounded below by approximation and estimation error on 3000 samples in a 4-D parameter space with sharp sensitivity. Log features linearise the exponential-like decay of the temperature traces, making the input-output map closer to linear for the MLP. The log-target transform enforces positivity. The MLP's error is small enough (relative error <~10%) to lie inside the LM convergence basin 10 LM iterations from a good start reach the same stationary point as a converged multistart Temperatures at the sensors stay strictly positive (a Gaussian pulse diffusing with Dirichlet ends), so log features are well defined; the harness handles any clipping The forward model matches the simulator used to generate the data

assumptions: The MLP's error is small enough (relative error <~10%) to lie inside the LM convergence basin
10 LM iterations from a good start reach the same stationary point as a converged multistart
Temperatures at the sensors stay strictly positive (a Gaussian pulse diffusing with Dirichlet ends), so log features are well defined; the harness handles any clipping
The forward model matches the simulator used to generate the data
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 for the MLP initializer alone vs the hybrid. The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid improves on the MLP by less than 30%, or if the hybrid's val rel_l2 exceeds 0.05.
data.if_fails: If the hybrid shows no improvement over the MLP, then either LM is not converging in 10 iterations, implying stronger nonlinearity or worse conditioning than the median suggests, or the MLP is already near the CRB, implying the regression is efficient. Per-parameter errors versus the CRB distinguish the two. If the MLP init is worse than the prior centre, log features are corrupted by near-zero or negative noisy temperatures; switch to raw features.

author: researcher-ml
title: Learned initializer + few-step Levenberg–Marquardt refinement (hybrid) should approach the Cramér–Rao floor
text: Initialize from a cheap learned inverse map (kernel ridge on standardized raw sensor traces). Then run about 10 bounded LM iterations through the exact forward model in log-k space, with posterior-mean estimation under the box prior. This should reach test-proxy (val) rel_l2 < 0.035, within ~1.8x of the CRB floor of 0.0195. It should also beat the best purely data-driven method by at least 30% relative. The forward model is cheap (40-point explicit FD, 200 steps) and available, the noise is small (sigma = 1e-3), and the median Fisher condition number is only 46.6. So the likelihood near the truth should be close to quadratic in log k, and Gauss–Newton/LM should converge in a few iterations from a reasonable start. A learned initializer removes most of the risk of multistart failure and local minima at a fraction of full multistart cost. The posterior-mean estimator should help k1 and k4, which have the largest CRB relative std and the most prior-boundary pull. The log transform enforces positivity and evens out the curvature across the [0.5, 2] range. The forward model used by the harness is the data-generating simulator, so there is no model misspecification. The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 1e-3, so least squares is the MLE. Kernel ridge gives initial estimates inside the LM basin of attraction (rel error well under ~0.2). 10 LM iterations over 750 val + 750 test samples fit inside the 120 s per-experiment limit.

assumptions: The forward model used by the harness is the data-generating simulator, so there is no model misspecification.
The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 1e-3, so least squares is the MLE.
Kernel ridge gives initial estimates inside the LM basin of attraction (rel error well under ~0.2).
10 LM iterations over 750 val + 750 test samples fit inside the 120 s per-experiment limit.
data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 of the hybrid against the initializer alone and against the CRB floor. The hypothesis is falsified if hybrid val rel_l2 >= 0.035, or if it fails to improve on the initializer alone by >= 30%.
data.if_fails: If refinement does not close the gap, the cause is one of three things: the initializer lands outside the basin (check per-sample residual chi^2), the Laplace/importance-sampling posterior mean is biased near the box edges, or the simulator differs from the data generator (residuals well above sigma^2 per reading). Each cause points to a different fix: multistart, the MAP estimator, or a learned correction.

author: researcher-ml
title: Amortized neural inverse map with log-target and noise augmentation reaches the success threshold without forward-model calls at test time
text: A torch MLP trained on 3000 simulated pairs should reach val rel_l2 < 0.06 and land within a factor of ~3 of the CRB floor. The inputs are PCA-compressed standardized sensor traces; the targets are log k; training uses on-the-fly re-noising at the known sigma. The model is limited mainly by sample count rather than noise. The prediction is that it stays worse than the hybrid of proposal 1 by more than 25%. The inverse map from noise-free traces to log k is smooth and low-dimensional (4 outputs), and the sensor traces are strongly correlated in time, so PCA should keep the informative subspace. Training on log targets matches the multiplicative scale of conductivity and the rel_l2 metric. Re-noising at sigma = 1e-3 regularizes the map toward the posterior mean rather than toward memorizing the noise in the training set. This tests whether amortized ML alone is competitive with physics refinement at this data size. That result matters for problems where forward calls at test time are expensive. 3000 training samples cover the 4-D prior box densely enough for a smooth MLP; this is roughly 7-8 samples per axis. PCA with 64 components retains the Fisher-informative directions. Small-variance directions carrying k1/k4 information could be lost, and this is a risk. noise_scale is interpreted in raw feature units, matching sigma = 1e-3.

assumptions: 3000 training samples cover the 4-D prior box densely enough for a smooth MLP; this is roughly 7-8 samples per axis.
PCA with 64 components retains the Fisher-informative directions. Small-variance directions carrying k1/k4 information could be lost, and this is a risk.
noise_scale is interpreted in raw feature units, matching sigma = 1e-3.
data.falsifiable_test: Train and evaluate on val. The hypothesis is falsified if val rel_l2 >= 0.06. Separately, the comparative claim is falsified if the MLP comes within 25% of the hybrid. Also report per-parameter relative error: the prediction is that the k1/k4 errors exceed the k2/k3 errors by more than 2x, mirroring the CRB ordering.
data.if_fails: If the MLP matches or beats the hybrid, the LM refinement is wasted compute and amortized inference is sufficient. If the MLP is far worse than 0.06, either PCA is discarding the k1/k4 information (retry with pca=0 or more components) or the sample size is limiting. In that case, generating extra simulated training data via a custom_solver using context.forward is the next experiment.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Well-specified forward model makes per-sample MLE reach the CRB floor: LM in log-k with multistart
text: Because the forward model is available, noise is known i.i.d. Gaussian (sigma=0.001), and the Fisher matrix is well-conditioned (median cond 46.6), bounded Levenberg-Marquardt in log-k with a few starts will converge to the global least-squares minimum for nearly every sample. Its test rel_l2 should then be close to the CRB floor (~0.02), and clearly below 0.05. With a correctly specified simulator and only 4 parameters, a learned regressor trained on 3000 samples must interpolate a 4-D inverse map. Its error then has two parts: noise propagation plus approximation and variance error. Per-sample MLE has only the noise-propagation term, asymptotically at the CRB. The log transform enforces positivity and makes the parameterisation better matched to multiplicative sensitivity of u to k. Multistart guards against local minima caused by the k1/k4 near-flat directions. Residual whiteness at sigma is a direct model-fidelity control. context.forward is the same simulator that generated the data, with the same grid, dt, initial condition and sensor indices (no model discrepancy). The explicit scheme is stable over the whole prior box (k<=2 with 40 points and 200 steps), so the forward map is smooth. Noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with known sigma, so least squares is the MLE. The forward-call budget allows about 750 samples x (3 starts x ~20 iters) on top of Jacobians within 120s per experiment.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Under rel_l2 loss, the MMSE posterior mean beats the MLE on the weakly identified edge segments (competing-explanation control)
text: The rel_l2 metric is a squared-error loss, and k1/k4 have relatively large posterior spread with the uniform box prior truncating it. So the posterior mean under the box prior (MAP-start LM, then importance sampling on the Laplace approximation) will give lower val rel_l2 than the mode estimate from Proposal 1. The gain should concentrate in k1 and k4 and in samples near the bounds [0.5, 2.0]. A learned-init hybrid (ridge on log features into LM) should match it at lower cost. The two proposals separate two explanations for any residual gap above the CRB floor. Explanation A: optimisation failure or local minima, which the hybrid init fixes. Explanation B: estimator choice under the posterior geometry, which posterior_mean fixes. Box truncation of a posterior with about 2% relative std is small mid-box but non-negligible near the edges, where the MLE can sit on a bound. A cheap ridge initializer on log temperatures is near-linear in log-k for diffusion data, which should cut the iterations and starts needed. The comparison should stratify the per-parameter error by distance to the bound. The Laplace (Gauss-Newton) approximation is accurate enough as an importance proposal (posterior std about 2%, so the posterior is nearly Gaussian in log-k). The data-generating prior really is uniform on [0.5, 2]^4, so the box-prior MMSE is the Bayes-optimal estimator for squared error. Ridge on log-sensor features gives an initializer within the LM basin of attraction for most samples.

data.falsifiable_test: Compare against the Proposal 1 physics/mode run on the same val set, using a paired bootstrap over samples for rel_l2. The prediction is that this method's val rel_l2 is lower by at least 3% relative, and that the per-parameter gain is larger for k1 and k4 than for k2 and k3. Falsified if the paired bootstrap 95% CI for the difference includes 0 or favours the mode, or if the gain is not concentrated in k1/k4 and the near-bound samples.
data.if_fails: If there is no gain, the posterior is effectively untruncated and Gaussian, so the mode is sufficient and the remaining error is pure noise at the CRB. In that case, spend the budget on confirming fidelity rather than on estimator choice. If the hybrid is worse than multistart physics, the ridge init falls outside the basin for some samples, which points to multimodality in the k1/k4 directions.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: MMSE beats MLE: learned initializer + LM refinement with a box-prior posterior-mean estimator in log-conductivity space
text: Rel_l2 is a squared-error-type loss, so the Bayes-optimal point estimate under the uniform box prior is the posterior mean, not the MLE or mode. A hybrid that starts from a learned initializer, refines by bounded LM in log(k), and then reports the importance-sampled posterior mean will reach val rel_l2 <= 0.025, close to the CRB floor estimate of 0.0195. It will also beat the same pipeline with estimator='mode' by at least 5% relative, with the gain concentrated in k1 and k4, which are least determined and most likely to have posterior mass truncated at the 0.5/2.0 bounds. This challenges the default framing that the inverse problem means finding the data-fitting theta. With Fisher condition number about 47 and CR relative std of about 2% on k1 and k4, the posteriors are narrow but not negligible. For draws near the box edges, the Laplace Gaussian is truncated, and the MLE is biased relative to the conditional mean. A posterior-mean estimator combines the statistical-decision-theory tradition (Bayes risk under the evaluation loss) with the numerical-PDE tradition (Gauss-Newton through the forward model). The learned initializer replaces expensive multistart: a 4-parameter map from 4 sensor time series should be smooth enough for kernel ridge to land in the basin of the global minimum. That saves compute under the 400 worker-second budget. The forward model is cheap enough (explicit FD, 40 points, 200 steps) that about 10 LM iterations plus 64 importance samples for each of 750 val samples fit within the 120 s per-experiment limit on 6 workers. The misfit landscape is unimodal near the kernel-ridge initial guess. Piecewise-constant k with 4 segments and sensors in each segment makes gross non-identifiability unlikely, but this is not proven. The Laplace approximation in log(k) is a good enough importance proposal that 64 samples give low-variance posterior-mean estimates. The noise model (i.i.d. Gaussian, sigma = 0.001) is exactly the one used in simulation, so the likelihood is correctly specified.

Either would be a significant finding. If posterior_mean is about equal to mode, the problem is effectively in the asymptotic regime where Bayesian refinements are irrelevant, and future effort should go to speed rather than estimator design.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Spectral reformulation: log-temperature features turn late-time decay into a near-linear function of log(k)
text: The inverse map is far more linear in (log u, log k) coordinates than in raw coordinates. At late times, the Dirichlet solution decays as a sum of modes with rates set by the Sturm–Liouville eigenvalues of -(k u')'. Those eigenvalues scale roughly multiplicatively with k, so log-temperatures are approximately affine in time with slopes that are smooth functions of log k. A purely data-driven model that never calls the forward model at prediction time, trained on log-transformed features with a log target and noise augmentation, will reach val rel_l2 <= 0.05. It will also outperform the same model on raw features by at least 30% relative. This challenges the assumption that this is a generic regression on raw time series, or else that it requires PDE solves at prediction time. It borrows from spectral theory and system identification: decay rates are the natural sufficient statistics of a diffusion with known initial condition, and the log transform exposes them. If the hypothesis holds, an amortized estimator nearly matches the physics solver at a tiny fraction of the cost, which matters under the 400 worker-second budget. The torch MLP is the flexible learner. Noise augmentation at sigma = 0.001 keeps it from overfitting to noiseless structure that the log transform would amplify at small temperatures. Sensor readings remain well above the noise floor (about 0.001) for most of the time window. Otherwise log features amplify noise and the advantage turns into a disadvantage. Sensors at indices 5 and 35 near the Dirichlet ends are most at risk. The harness 'log' feature set handles non-positive noisy readings safely, for example by clipping or an offset. 3000 training samples suffice for an MLP to learn a smooth 4-parameter inverse map. If the map is near-linear in log space, this is easily enough. Train, val and test share the same prior and noise distribution.

If both feature sets plateau well above 0.05, the amortized map is too nonlinear or under-sampled at n = 3000, and per-sample refinement through the forward model is necessary.

The amortised init replaces multistart's job of finding the basin. If accuracy matches P-001, the learned map has bought cost, not accuracy, and that is the expected outcome. This is to be checked by the forward-fidelity control the critic requested (residual std/sigma close to 1). The noise is i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 1e-3, so least squares is the MLE. Unscaled PCA(32) retains the Fisher-informative directions for k1/k4. title: Log-temperature features for an amortised MLP: single arm of a merged log/raw pair with P-011, gated on a ridge pilot
text:
Short-time heterogeneous asymptotics give log u ~ c(t) - d^2/(4t) with d = integral of dx/sqrt(k). Log features therefore make the inverse map closer to linear than raw features do.
(a) Ridge on log features beats ridge on raw features in val rel_l2, with the gain concentrated in k2/k3.
(b) A torch MLP on log features, matched to P-011 in architecture, reaches val rel_l2 <= 0.05 and beats P-011 (raw) by at least 15%.
(c) For k1/k4 the log advantage is under 5% or reversed, because edge sensors sit near the noise floor early in the window. This challenges the assumption that raw traces are the right coordinates for an amortised inverse. The per-parameter signature in (c) separates the travel-time mechanism from a generic claim that log features help. Merging with P-011 halves the budget the critic flagged. Short-time regime: T <= about 0.033, so many modes are active and the near-front behaviour dominates. The harness should report dt and T. The harness log feature handles readings at or below 0 by clipping or an offset, and noise_aug is applied in raw space before the transform. P-011 uses hidden=[256,256], silu, lr=1e-3, wd=1e-4, batch=128, the same epochs and noise_aug=2. Otherwise the pair is not matched. 3000 samples are enough for an MLP to get within about 2.5x of the CRB on a smooth 4-D map.

data.falsifiable_test:
Pilot (about 5 s): ridge on log versus raw features, with per-parameter val relative errors and the per-sensor fraction of readings at or below 3*sigma. The MLP is run only if (a) holds. The main comparison is against P-011 at identical settings, with 2 seeds if budget allows.

The hypothesis is refuted if any of the following holds:
(a) Log ridge does not beat raw ridge.
(b) MLP val rel_l2 is above 0.05.
(c) The MLP gain over P-011 is under 15%.
(d) The k1/k4 gain exceeds the k2/k3 gain.
data.if_fails: If (a) fails, log coordinates do not linearise the map at these times or noise levels, and amortised effort should go to raw features plus PCA. If (a) holds but (b) or (c) fail, the MLP absorbs the representation difference, so feature choice matters only for linear or kernel models. If (d) fails, the edge sensors are not noise-limited, and the travel-time picture is wrong for the outer segments.
data.response_to_critic:
(1) Mechanism refinement: accepted. It improves the hypothesis. The heterogeneous short-time asymptotic is log u(x,t) ~ c(t) - d(x)^2/(4t), with d = integral of dx/sqrt(k). Across the time window, the log trace at each sensor is affine in 1/t with slope -d^2. d is linear in the segment values k_i^{-1/2}, weighted by path length. So the most linearising target is k^{-1/2}, not log k. Library specs only allow none/log targets, so I moved that test into a new custom_ml proposal (KRR with log features and a k^{-1/2} target). This proposal keeps the log-vs-raw feature question.

(2) Edge noise and clipping: accepted. I cannot see how the harness 'log' feature treats non-positive readings. The new proposal therefore implements its own explicit clip at 3*sigma in raw space before the log. Noise augmentation there is applied in raw space by construction. For this library arm, I add the assumption that noise_aug is applied before the feature transform, and I keep the prediction that k1/k4 gain little or lose.

(3) Budget duplication with P-011: accepted. I drop my own raw twin. P-016 becomes the single log-feature arm of a merged pair with P-011, using an identical architecture and seed han

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Travel-time target coordinate: KRR on clipped log traces predicting k^{-1/2} instead of log k
text:
Because log u ~ c(t) - d^2/(4t) with d = sum_i L_i * k_i^{-1/2}, the map from log traces to k^{-1/2} is smoother than the map to log k.
(a) Ridge on clipped log features with a k^{-1/2} target beats the same ridge with a log-k target by at least 10% in val rel_l2.
(b) The KRR spec below beats the identical KRR with a log-k target by at least 5%, or is within 2% of it if the kernel absorbs the curvature.
(c) KRR(k^{-1/2}) reaches val rel_l2 < 0.06 as a pure amortised model. The critic's Varadhan-type refinement predicts a specific natural coordinate. Choosing the target coordinate is a cheap, nonstandard lever that the library specs cannot express. The explicit 3*sigma clip in raw space also removes the ambiguity in the harness log feature that the critic flagged. If (a) holds, it also tells P-010, P-015 and other hybrids that a k^{-1/2}-target initializer is the better amortised starting point. The short-time asymptotic is approximately valid over a substantial part of the window, at least for the inner sensors. A clip floor of 3e-3 (3*sigma) keeps the log noise bounded. Readings below the floor carry little information. The raw features passed in are the noisy sensor traces in the harness layout. Clipping is per-entry, so the layout does not matter. Target pairs cover the prior box. The inverse transform 1/z^2 is clipped to [0.5, 2].

data.falsifiable_test:
Run four cheap arms with the same code: linear in {True, False} x target in {'invsqrt', 'log'}. Total about 15 s.

The hypothesis is refuted if any of the following holds:
(a) Linear invsqrt does not beat linear log by at least 10%.
(b) KRR invsqrt is more than 2% worse than KRR log.
(c) KRR invsqrt val rel_l2 is 0.06 or higher.

Report per-parameter errors to check whether the gain sits in k2/k3, as the travel-time picture predicts.
data.if_fails: If the linear arms show no target-coordinate effect, the short-time travel-time asymptotic does not describe this window. That would mean the explicit-FD T is long enough for boundary and multi-mode corrections to dominate, which also undercuts the P-016 mechanism. If the linear arms show the effect but KRR does not, the coordinate matters only for low-capacity models and initializers.
